blocks.text: 95% of women have mild **PMS** symptoms; 5% suffer severe symptoms; severe **PMS** affects 3-8% of women of reproductive age. Comorbidity with a mood disorder is seen in 30-70%; **PMDD** carries a higher risk of postnatal depression.

source.file: books/7-3-liaison-psychiatry.pdf

blocks.text: **PMDD** (**DSM-5**) requires ≥5 of 11 symptoms (including ≥1 of depressed mood/marked anxiety/marked affective lability/marked anger-irritability) present in most cycles over the past year, confined to the last week of the luteal phase, remitting within days of menses onset, confirmed by prospective daily ratings over ≥2 cycles. Breast tenderness/bloating are not seen in major depressive disorder and help distinguish **PMDD**.

source.file: books/7-3-liaison-psychiatry.pdf

blocks.forTopic: PMDD diagnostic criteria (DSM-5) - core symptom cluster
blocks.mnemonic: "DAAL" for the four core symptoms, one of which must be present
expansion: Lability of anger/irritability (marked, usually most severe, starts earliest)

blocks.text: Aetiology: increased sensitivity to normal gonadal-hormone fluctuation (not a drop in progesterone). Serotonin has a pathogenic role; **GABA-A**/progesterone-metabolite interaction is also implicated.

source.file: books/7-3-liaison-psychiatry.pdf

blocks.text: SSRIs (**fluoxetine** most studied/most effective, also **sertraline**, **citalopram**, **escitalopram**, **clomipramine**, **venlafaxine**) have a 60-90% response rate vs 30-40% placebo (Dimmock 2000 meta-analysis **OR** 6.91). Effects appear within one cycle - too rapid to be a classic antidepressant mechanism.

source.file: books/7-3-liaison-psychiatry.pdf

blocks.text: Intermittent luteal-phase dosing is effective only during the 2 weeks pre-menses, is cheaper, has fewer withdrawal effects, and is more effective than continuous/semi-continuous dosing (Wikander 1998) for core symptoms, though less effective than continuous dosing for somatic symptoms. No significant difference between continuous and intermittent dosing overall (Dimmock 2000).

source.file: books/7-3-liaison-psychiatry.pdf

blocks.text: **SSRI** in **PMS** differs from **SSRI** in depression: low (not high) frequency of sexual side effects, intermittent (not continuous) dosing more effective, effective within days (not 3-4 weeks), no reported akathisia/increased suicidal ideation.

source.file: books/7-3-liaison-psychiatry.pdf

blocks.title: PDD/PMS versus depression response to SSRIs

blocks.text: Hormonal suppression of ovulation (GnRH agonist, oestrogen, some contraceptives) should be reserved as a last resort given early-menopause implications. Remission on stopping treatment is low; **PMS** can persist until menopause.

source.file: books/7-3-liaison-psychiatry.pdf

blocks.text: 20% of coronary heart disease patients have comorbid depression (Ramamurthy 2013). Psychological/behavioural interventions reduce depression and mortality in **CAD** (Welton 2009); persistent depression despite treatment raises cardiac risk (**OR** 1.53, Nicholson 2006).

source.file: books/7-3-liaison-psychiatry.pdf

blocks.text: **SADHART** (**sertraline** vs placebo, 16 weeks, post-**MI** depression) showed no safety difference (**LVEF**, PVCs, QTc) and a nonsignificant reduction in **MI**/**CHD** death with **sertraline** (**RR** 0.77, 95% **CI** 0.51-1.16), suggesting possible cardioprotection via reduced platelet activation; benefit was greater in severe/recurrent depression.

source.file: books/7-3-liaison-psychiatry.pdf

blocks.text: **ENRICHD** (**CBT**) and **MIND-IT** trials had only modest effects on depression and neither improved survival.

source.file: books/7-3-liaison-psychiatry.pdf

blocks.text: Depression prevalence in **CHF** is ~21.5% (~19% meet formal **MDD** criteria) - about 2-3x (risk ratio 3:1) the general-population rate; similar in inpatients and outpatients, higher with higher **NYHA** class and in women. Relative mortality risk in depressed **CHF** patients is ~2:1 vs non-depressed **CHF** patients.

source.file: books/7-3-liaison-psychiatry.pdf

blocks.text: Depression risk in **CHF** versus the general population is quoted as an exact 3:1 ratio (21.5% prevalence) - option lists offer nearby-sounding wrong ratios (1:8, 5:1, 1:7, 1:5) to test precise recall.

blocks.text: **Sertraline** is the drug of choice for depression following **MI** (best trial evidence, **SADHART**); avoid **fluvoxamine** and **citalopram**/**escitalopram**. Antidepressants are best avoided in the first 2 months post-**MI**; if sedation is needed, consider **mirtazapine** or low-dose **trazodone**.

source.file: question_bank/Clinical Parts_ Paper B/MCQs Liaison Part 1_ Attempt review.pdf

blocks.text: Post-**MI** depression: **sertraline** (**SADHART**) is the drug of choice - **fluvoxamine** and **citalopram**/**escitalopram** should specifically be avoided, and antidepressants are generally avoided in the first 2 months post-**MI** regardless of drug choice.

source.file: question_bank/Clinical Parts_ Paper B/MCQs Liaison Part 1_ Attempt review.pdf

blocks.text: Hyperthyroidism: most commonly generalized anxiety; also depression, irritability, hypomania, cognitive dysfunction; mania can occur in severe thyrotoxicosis. Hypothyroidism: M:F ratio 1:6; depression often misdiagnosed as primary **MDD**, myxoedema madness (psychosis) in severe cases; subclinical hypothyroidism is a risk factor for depression and for rapid cycling in bipolar disorder.

source.file: books/7-3-liaison-psychiatry.pdf

blocks.text: Hyperparathyroidism symptoms track serum calcium: mild-moderate (10-14 mg/dL) causes depression/apathy/irritability; severe (>14 mg/dL) causes delirium with psychosis, catatonia, or lethargy progressing to coma. Hypoparathyroidism: mild hypocalcaemia causes anxiety/paraesthesias/irritability/lability; severe causes mania, psychosis, tetany, seizures.

source.file: books/7-3-liaison-psychiatry.pdf

blocks.text: Cushing's syndrome (cortisol excess, most commonly exogenous steroids; pituitary source = Cushing's disease): psychiatric symptoms may precede physical signs; depression is the most common symptom, followed by anxiety, hypomania/mania, psychosis, cognitive dysfunction. Exogenous steroids produce more mania than endogenous excess; effects are often dose-related.

source.file: books/7-3-liaison-psychiatry.pdf

blocks.text: Addison's disease (cortisol depletion): apathy, anhedonia, fatigue, depressed mood (may mimic primary **MDD**) - but nausea, vomiting, and skin pigmentation changes point to Addison's rather than depression.

source.file: books/7-3-liaison-psychiatry.pdf

blocks.text: Pheochromocytoma (catecholamine-secreting tumour): episodic tachycardia, labile hypertension, headache, sweating, palpitations that can mimic panic attacks. Screen with urinary catecholamines (**VMA**, metanephrines); the best diagnostic test is a plasma metanephrine level (more specific).

source.file: books/7-3-liaison-psychiatry.pdf

blocks.text: Depression is 2-3x more common in diabetics than the general population and is linked to poorer glycaemic control and more complications. Type 2 diabetes prevalence is 2-4x higher in bipolar disorder/schizophrenia/severe depression. Recurrent hypoglycaemia rarely causes permanent cognitive dysfunction; frequent hyperglycaemia causing cerebral micro/macrovascular damage is the more common route to cognitive impairment.

source.file: books/7-3-liaison-psychiatry.pdf

blocks.text: Subclinical hypothyroidism (not hyper/hypoparathyroidism, hyperthyroidism, or hypopituitarism) is the specific risk factor tested for both depression and rapid cycling in bipolar disorder.

source.file: question_bank/Clinical Parts_ Paper B/MCQs Liaison Part 2_ Attempt review.pdf

blocks.text: **SLE** can present as a mood disorder mimicking bipolar disorder - a vignette with elated/manic mood plus a sun-worsened facial rash and mouth ulcers should trigger consideration of **SLE**, not primary bipolar disorder.

source.file: question_bank/Clinical Parts_ Paper B/MCQs Liaison Part 1_ Attempt review.pdf

sections.title: 4. Renal Medicine: Psychotropic Prescribing & Uraemic Syndromes

blocks.text: **Diazepam**'s half-life is unchanged in end-stage renal disease but its metabolite desmethyldiazepam accumulates. **Lorazepam**'s half-life rises from 8-25h (normal) to 32-72h in end-stage renal disease; reduce dose by 50% at low renal function to avoid excessive sedation.

source.file: books/7-3-liaison-psychiatry.pdf

blocks.text: **Imipramine**/**amitriptyline**: usual dosage in renal impairment (half-life unaffected). **Citalopram**: half the normal dose in renal impairment/elderly. **Paroxetine** half-life is considerably increased in severe renal impairment (reduce dose). **Fluoxetine**/**fluvoxamine**: no dose reduction needed in elderly or renal impairment. **Sertraline**: manufacturer does not recommend use in renal impairment.

source.file: books/7-3-liaison-psychiatry.pdf

blocks.text: **Haloperidol** needs no dose reduction in renal impairment unless sedation/hypotension occur. **Amisulpride** is almost exclusively renally excreted, so renal failure is a relative contraindication (alternate-day dosing/dose reduction if no alternative). **Risperidone** and its active metabolite are substantially renally excreted, prolonging elimination half-life in renal impairment. **Lithium** is best avoided or used at low dose in renal impairment.

source.file: books/7-3-liaison-psychiatry.pdf

blocks.text: Uraemic encephalopathy occurs when **GFR** falls to 10% of normal; onset rate tracks the rate of **GFR** decline; causes cognitive/psychomotor/personality change with vomiting, restlessness, myoclonus, coma - reversible with dialysis, transplant, or treating the underlying disease.

source.file: books/7-3-liaison-psychiatry.pdf

blocks.text: Dialysis disequilibrium syndrome occurs during/after early dialysis sessions, more common in younger patients and those with pre-existing neurological problems (cerebral trauma, recent stroke); mild symptoms (headache, restlessness) can progress to nausea, vomiting, hypertension, tremor, disorientation, seizures - mostly secondary to cerebral oedema. Now less common with improved dialysis technology.

source.file: books/7-3-liaison-psychiatry.pdf

blocks.text: Major depression prevalence in advanced cancer is 5-15% (another 10-15% have less severe symptoms). Somatic symptoms are not useful for diagnosing depression here; pervasive global anhedonia is the more useful criterion.

source.file: books/7-3-liaison-psychiatry.pdf

blocks.text: **SSRI** evidence in palliative depression is limited/not well established; low-dose **amitriptyline** is useful if neuropathic pain is present but should be avoided in those at higher delirium risk; **lofepramine** and rapid-acting psychostimulants (dexamphetamine, **methylphenidate**) are useful, particularly for patients with only weeks of life.

source.file: books/7-3-liaison-psychiatry.pdf

blocks.text: Delirium prevalence in cancer inpatients is ~44%, rising to 62% shortly before death; aetiology is usually multifactorial and a specific cause is found in <50% of terminally ill patients. Low-dose **haloperidol** or **lorazepam** is frequently used but not always successful, especially in the hypoactive (sedated) subtype.

source.file: books/7-3-liaison-psychiatry.pdf

blocks.text: "**SSRI** evidence in palliative depression is well established" is the deliberately false statement in an except-question - the true position is that **SSRI** evidence here is feeble/largely empirical, contrasted with **amitriptyline** (useful for neuropathic pain but delirium risk), **lorazepam** (acute anxiety), and **risperidone** (psychotic symptoms in the terminally ill).

source.file: question_bank/Clinical Parts_ Paper B/MCQs Liaison Part 1_ Attempt review.pdf

blocks.text: **SSRI** evidence for depression in palliative care is described as feeble/largely empirical - the exam marks "**SSRI** evidence here is well established" as the false statement, contrasted with **amitriptyline** (neuropathic pain but delirium risk), **lorazepam** (acute anxiety), and **risperidone** (psychotic symptoms).

source.file: question_bank/Clinical Parts_ Paper B/MCQs Liaison Part 1_ Attempt review.pdf

blocks.text: In terminal illness, depression is not uncommon and is not easily diagnosed; somatic symptoms do not strongly favour the diagnosis (the opposite is true - anhedonia is more useful); amphetamines (dexamphetamine/**methylphenidate**) can be used for depression when only weeks of life remain.

sections.title: 6. Other Medical Disorders with Neuropsychiatric Presentations

blocks.text: Lyme disease (Borrelia burgdorferi via tick bite): erythema migrans develops within 4 weeks; ~15% develop neuroborreliosis (rare in **UK**, more common in North America) with back pain worse at night, facial numbness/palsy. Late-stage disease can cause memory impairment, word-finding problems, psychosis, seizures, violent behaviour, anxiety, depression - can mimic any encephalopathy/psychiatric disorder, often compared to neurosyphilis.

source.file: books/7-3-liaison-psychiatry.pdf

blocks.text: **SLE**: nonorgan-specific vasculitis with antinuclear antibodies; butterfly rash, joint/kidney/serosal injury. Depression and anxiety common, particularly early after diagnosis and with disfiguring skin lesions; psychosis is rare. **CNS** manifestations include peripheral neuropathy (rarely Guillain-Barre), grand mal seizures, chorea, cognitive impairment, severe headache, stroke, B-cell lymphoma, and a limbic-encephalitis-type picture.

source.file: books/7-3-liaison-psychiatry.pdf

blocks.text: Insulinoma (a common pancreatic neuroendocrine tumour) can present with neuropsychiatric symptoms often misdiagnosed as psychosis/depression; classically recurrent headache, lethargy, diplopia and blurred vision, particularly with exercise or fasting.

source.file: books/7-3-liaison-psychiatry.pdf

blocks.text: Neurosarcoidosis: idiopathic granulomas (mainly lung/mediastinal nodes) that can affect cranial nerves (bilateral facial palsy); depression in 20%, psychosis rare; erythema nodosum on the shin is a cutaneous sign; **ACE** levels elevated from macrophage activity; treated with immunosuppression.

source.file: books/7-3-liaison-psychiatry.pdf

blocks.text: Metachromatic leucodystrophy (arylsulfatase A deficiency) has infantile, juvenile, and adult forms; nearly 60% of adolescent-onset cases have schizophrenia-like psychosis (not seen in younger-onset cases); the adult form commonly begins after age 16 as a psychiatric disorder or progressive dementia.

source.file: books/7-3-liaison-psychiatry.pdf

blocks.text: Neuroacanthocytosis: movement disorder/ataxia with personality change (impulsivity, distractibility, anxiety, depression, apathy), cognitive deterioration, axonal neuropathy, seizures; acanthocytosis affects typically 10-30% of erythrocytes; subcortical dementia may develop.

source.file: books/7-3-liaison-psychiatry.pdf

blocks.text: Onset age 20-40; **UK** lifetime risk 1:8000; twice as common in women; incidence rises with distance from the equator. Predominantly white-matter disease with plaques in optic nerves, cerebellum, brain stem, spinal cord. 5-10% primary progressive (no remission); 20-30% relapsing-remitting without serious disability; 60% secondary progressive after relapses/remissions.

source.file: books/7-3-liaison-psychiatry.pdf

blocks.text: Depression lifetime prevalence 40-50% (~3x general population), linked to poorer cognitive function, poor treatment compliance, lower quality of life. Drug-induced low mood is an important differential: steroids (more likely), baclofen, dantrolene, tizanidine. Interferon-**ALPHA** (used in viral hepatitis) - not beta-interferon - is the one clearly linked to depression; the beta-interferon association is controversial/contested.

source.file: books/7-3-liaison-psychiatry.pdf

blocks.text: Desipramine and SSRIs have an evidence base for **MS** depression. **ECT** may be used but carries a 20% risk of triggering an **MS** relapse; active **MRI** lesions before treatment are a risk factor for relapse post-**ECT** - **ECT** is not absolutely contraindicated. Suicide accounts for 3% of **MS** deaths over 6 years and 15% over 16 years; suicidal ideation is present cross-sectionally in nearly 30%.

source.file: books/7-3-liaison-psychiatry.pdf

blocks.text: Mania: higher-than-expected prevalence, can be drug-induced (steroids more likely than baclofen/dantrolene/tizanidine). Mild-to-moderate mania occurs in up to 1/3rd (not 2/3rd) of steroid-treated patients; steroid-induced hypomania is linked to family/premorbid affective disorder and/or alcoholism history.

source.file: books/7-3-liaison-psychiatry.pdf

blocks.text: **MRI** evidence shows mania-with-psychotic-symptoms plaques distributed predominantly in the bilateral **TEMPORAL** **HORN** areas (not a frontal distribution).

source.file: books/7-3-liaison-psychiatry.pdf

blocks.text: Pathological laughing/crying (emotionalism/pseudobulbar affect): mood-incongruent, involuntary; 66% of **MS** patients responded to **amitriptyline** 75mg/day in one study; amantadine, **levodopa**, **fluoxetine**, **sertraline**, and **citalopram** have also shown benefit.

source.file: books/7-3-liaison-psychiatry.pdf

items.text: **MS** steroid-induced mania: mild-to-moderate mania occurs in up to 1/3rd (not 2/3rd) of steroid-treated patients, and psychotic mania's plaques localise to the bilateral temporal horn (not a frontal distribution) - both figures are independently swapped as distractors across multiple questions.

source.file: question_bank/Clinical Parts_ Paper B/MCQs Liaison Part 2_ Attempt review.pdf

items.text: Beta-interferon's link to depression in **MS** is contested/controversial - the clearly depressogenic interferon is interferon-**ALPHA** (used in viral hepatitis), not beta. The exam expects steroids, not beta-interferon, as the answer for "most likely to cause depression" in **MS** treatment.

source.file: question_bank/Clinical Parts_ Paper B/MCQs Liaison Part 2_ Attempt review.pdf

items.text: **ECT** is **NOT** absolutely contraindicated in **MS** despite the 20% relapse-trigger risk - active **MRI** lesions pre-treatment are a risk factor for relapse, but this is a relative not absolute caution, a frequently misjudged "except" answer.

source.file: question_bank/Clinical Parts_ Paper B/MCQs Liaison Part 2_ Attempt review.pdf

blocks.text: Cognitive impairment in **MS** follows a subcortical pattern (not all patients affected; may predate neurological lesions); **MMSE** is not a useful screen; **donepezil** improved memory in an **RCT**. This subcortical-impairment profile is shared conceptually with other subcortical dementias (per Cummings & Benson) - it is not explained simply by depression prevalence and is not well screened by the **MMSE**.

source.file: question_bank/Clinical Parts_ Paper B/MCQs Liaison Part 2_ Attempt review.pdf

blocks.text: **MS** is characterised by diverse neurological signs from variable plaque distribution, twice as common in women, more frequent further from the equator, and 85-90% present with an acute neurological episode (e.g. optic neuritis); most follow a relapsing-remitting course - it is not uniform/progressive from onset and is not a bacterial illness.

source.file: question_bank/Clinical Parts_ Paper B/MCQs Liaison Part 1_ Attempt review.pdf

blocks.text: Post-stroke syndrome prevalences (Chemerinski & Robinson 2000): depression 35% (more subcortical lesions), anxiety 25% (more cortical lesions), mania rare, apathy without depression 20%, emotional incontinence 20%, catastrophic reaction 20%, psychosis rare.

source.file: books/7-3-liaison-psychiatry.pdf

blocks.title: Post-stroke psychiatric syndromes and prevalence (Chemerinski & Robinson, 2000)

blocks.text: Mean duration of post-stroke major depression is 34 weeks. Left-hemisphere-lesion depressogenicity has been contested recently; major depression is common with infarcts involving the basal ganglia, especially on the left.

source.file: books/7-3-liaison-psychiatry.pdf

blocks.text: National stroke mood guideline (Intercollegiate Working Group, 4th edn, 2012): screen for depression/anxiety in the first month; severe/persistent tearfulness (emotionalism) should be treated with antidepressants and monitored by crying frequency; continue antidepressants ≥4 months after initial recovery if response is good; do not use antidepressants routinely to prevent depression onset. Both **fluoxetine** and **citalopram** have **RCT** support, though **fluoxetine**'s effect has been inconsistent across trials.

source.file: books/7-3-liaison-psychiatry.pdf

blocks.text: Post-stroke antidepressant "best evidence" trap: different questions mark **nortriptyline** and **fluoxetine** as separately correct "best evidence" answers depending on the specific option list given - don't pattern-match to a single drug for post-stroke depression.

source.file: question_bank/Clinical Parts_ Paper B/MCQs Liaison Part 1_ Attempt review.pdf

blocks.text: Lesion proximity to the **LEFT** frontal lobe predicts post-stroke depression (Narushima 2003, Vataja 2004).

source.file: question_bank/Clinical Parts_ Paper B/MCQs Liaison Part 2_ Attempt review.pdf

blocks.text: Vascular depression presents with psychomotor retardation, anhedonia, lack of insight, and disability, but patients are **LESS** likely to report guilt than in primary depression; executive dysfunction is common.

source.file: question_bank/Clinical Parts_ Paper B/MCQs Liaison Part 1_ Attempt review.pdf

blocks.text: Symptom prevalences in epilepsy (Dilley & Fleminger 2006): depression 30-50%, panic disorder 20%, psychosis 3-7%. Depression is associated with stigma/demoralization and is especially common in temporal lobe epilepsy. Suicide risk is high even without depression (10-15% in some cohorts); mortality is nearly 25x higher when clinical depression is present.

source.file: books/7-3-liaison-psychiatry.pdf

blocks.text: SSRIs are first-line for depression in epilepsy (rare seizure-threshold reduction); **lithium** can increase seizure severity and reduce seizure threshold. Panic attacks can be interictal or periictal and must be differentiated from seizure activity.

source.file: books/7-3-liaison-psychiatry.pdf

blocks.text: Psychosis is more common in partial epilepsies; episodic psychosis is most often post-ictal (visual hallucinations more common than in functional psychosis). Antiepileptic-drug-related psychosis lasts <1 week; **vigabatrin** is especially associated with psychosis. **Sulpiride** and **haloperidol** may be less epileptogenic than other antipsychotics.

source.file: books/7-3-liaison-psychiatry.pdf

blocks.text: Pseudoseizures (non-epileptic seizures) associate with past psychiatric history, somatisation, and social stressors (esp. childhood abuse); more likely daytime and with others present; side-to-side head movement, tightly shut eyes (vs open eyes in true seizures), preserved body tone, rapid alertness/orientation recovery, and clear event recall. Incontinence has no diagnostic value; an abnormal **EEG** does not always mean epilepsy. Increased postictal serum prolactin (>1000 **IU**/l) supports true epilepsy but must be measured within 15 minutes.

source.file: books/7-3-liaison-psychiatry.pdf

blocks.text: **PNES** clues favouring it over epileptic seizures: closed eyes, duration >2 minutes (strongly suggestive if >10 min), coordinated side-to-side agonist-antagonist head/body movement - vs open eyes, automatisms, <30 second duration, and predictable anatomical progression favouring true epilepsy. Video-**EEG** telemetry is the best diagnostic measure; known epileptics **CAN** also have dissociative (non-epileptic) seizures.

source.file: question_bank/Clinical Parts_ Paper B/MCQs Liaison Part 1_ Attempt review.pdf

rows: Side-to-side head/body movement, coordinated agonist-antagonist activity
Often >2 min, strongly suggestive if >10 min

Detailed, clear recall of the event afterwards

blocks.text: Antipsychotic epileptogenicity: **sulpiride**, **haloperidol**, and **trifluoperazine** have low proconvulsant risk and suit epileptic psychosis; **chlorpromazine** is the most epileptogenic older drug (avoid); **clozapine** lowers the seizure threshold and requires caution.

source.file: question_bank/Clinical Parts_ Paper B/MCQs Liaison Part 2_ Attempt review.pdf

blocks.text: Antidepressant choice in epilepsy: **moclobemide** is not proconvulsant; SSRIs are generally a good choice; most TCAs (**amitriptyline**, dothiepin, **clomipramine**) and **bupropion** are epileptogenic and best avoided; **mirtazapine**, **venlafaxine**, **reboxetine**, and **duloxetine** should be used with care.

source.file: question_bank/Clinical Parts_ Paper B/MCQs Liaison Part 1_ Attempt review.pdf

blocks.text: Post-traumatic epilepsy occurs in 5% of closed and 30% of open head injuries (usually within the first year) and worsens prognosis.

source.file: question_bank/Clinical Parts_ Paper B/MCQs Liaison Part 2_ Attempt review.pdf

blocks.text: Psychiatric manifestation prevalences (Dilley & Fleminger 2006): all psychiatric symptoms 70%, depression 40-50%, hypomania/euphoria 2%/10%, anxiety 50-65%, apathy common, psychosis 40% (drug-related), cognitive impairment 19% (no dementia) / 25-40% dementia.

source.file: books/7-3-liaison-psychiatry.pdf

blocks.title: Psychiatric manifestations of Parkinson's disease (Dilley & Fleminger, 2006)

blocks.text: Depression risk factors: female gender, younger onset, prominent right-sided lesions, bradykinesia/gait disturbance, rapid disease progression, poorer cognitive status/ADLs. Apathy without depression is common and linked to executive dysfunction, and may be masked by Parkinsonian affect.

source.file: books/7-3-liaison-psychiatry.pdf

blocks.text: De novo mania is rare in **PD**; mania is mostly related to **levodopa**/dopamine-agonist treatment, especially with pre-existing bipolar disorder or family history. **Levodopa** can also cause pathological gambling, hypersexuality, and hallucinations. Psychosis is mostly drug-related (dopaminergic and anticholinergic); visual hallucinations occur in 20%, delusions in 3-30%.

source.file: books/7-3-liaison-psychiatry.pdf

blocks.text: Low-dose **clozapine** (<100mg/day) can improve psychosis without worsening Parkinsonism; **quetiapine** can also be used. Cognitive impairment risk factors: older age, late-onset **PD**, low socioeconomic status/education, severe extrapyramidal signs. Frontal-executive dysfunction with a subcortical dementia pattern is typical; Lewy body dementia is pathologically closely related and **rivastigmine** is useful there; no drug is yet licensed for **PD**-related dementia.

source.file: books/7-3-liaison-psychiatry.pdf

blocks.text: Cognitive-impairment risk factors are older age, **LATE**-onset **PD**, **LOW** socioeconomic status, **LOW** education, and severe extrapyramidal signs - younger age, early onset, high **SES**, and fewer extrapyramidal signs are the deliberate false-option pairings.

source.file: question_bank/Clinical Parts_ Paper B/MCQs Liaison Part 2_ Attempt review.pdf

blocks.text: **PD** cognitive-impairment risk factors are older age, **LATE**-onset **PD**, **LOW** socioeconomic status/education, and severe extrapyramidal signs - the reverse (younger, early-onset, high **SES**, fewer **EPS**) is the false-option set repeatedly used as distractors.

source.file: question_bank/Clinical Parts_ Paper B/MCQs Liaison Part 2_ Attempt review.pdf

blocks.text: The presence of cognitive impairment **WORSENS** **PD** prognosis (attention, concentration, problem-solving, and set-shifting deficits reflect frontal-cortical circuit dysfunction) - it does not improve outcome, a common distractor framing.

source.file: question_bank/Clinical Parts_ Paper B/MCQs Liaison Part 2_ Attempt review.pdf

blocks.text: The presence of cognitive impairment **WORSENS** **PD** prognosis, not improves it - a counter-intuitive-sounding "improves prognosis" distractor is offered.

source.file: question_bank/Clinical Parts_ Paper B/MCQs Liaison Part 2_ Attempt review.pdf

blocks.text: **Quetiapine** has evidence from 8 open-label studies (191 patients, ~80% improvement) and 2 single-blind RCTs showing efficacy similar to **clozapine** for **PD** psychosis not attributable to reducing **levodopa** dose.

source.file: question_bank/Clinical Parts_ Paper B/MCQs Liaison Part 2_ Attempt review.pdf

blocks.text: Autosomal dominant, high penetrance chorea/dystonia/incoordination/cognitive decline/behavioural difficulty disorder, often manifesting in middle age after affected individuals have had children. Psychiatric symptoms are present at first presentation in 30% of cases; 3-6% present first with a schizophreniform psychosis; **OCD**-like symptoms can occur from basal ganglia involvement. **MRI** shows caudate atrophy with box-car ventricles.

source.file: books/7-3-liaison-psychiatry.pdf

blocks.text: The **HD** gene (huntingtin, expanded **CAG** repeat) is on the **SHORT** arm of chromosome 4. ≥41 repeats = full penetrance; 36-40 repeats = incomplete penetrance (relatively rare, ~95% penetrance even at 36-39 repeats); ≤35 repeats not associated with disease. **CAG** repeat number explains ~60% of variation in age of onset. Inheritance shows anticipation.

source.file: books/7-3-liaison-psychiatry.pdf

blocks.title: Huntington's disease: CAG repeat length and penetrance
rows: Incomplete penetrance (relatively rare; ~95% penetrance even at 36-39)

blocks.text: Suicide rate in **HD** is 4x the general population; unaffected family members also carry elevated suicide risk, at times as high as affected patients.

source.file: books/7-3-liaison-psychiatry.pdf

blocks.text: Lifetime suicide risk in **HD** is quoted as 10-15% (also expressed as 4-6x general-population rate, up to 12.7%, rising further after age 50); suicide is the 3rd commonest cause of death in **HD** after pneumonia and cardiovascular disease - don't conflate this absolute lifetime-risk figure with the separate relative-risk multiplier from the book notes.

source.file: question_bank/Clinical Parts_ Paper B/MCQs Liaison Part 2_ Attempt review.pdf

blocks.text: The most common behavioural change in **HD** (Craufurd 2001) is lack of initiative, followed by poor judgement, blunted affect, poor self-care, self-centredness, and inflexibility; irritability/impulsivity/verbal outbursts occur in 15-60% - disinhibition/aggression/agitation are **NOT** the most common change, a frequent distractor.

source.file: question_bank/Clinical Parts_ Paper B/MCQs Liaison Part 2_ Attempt review.pdf

items.text: The Huntington's disease gene sits on the **SHORT** arm of chromosome 4 - option lists commonly swap in "long arm" as the wrong answer.

source.file: question_bank/Clinical Parts_ Paper B/MCQs Liaison Part 2_ Attempt review.pdf

items.text: Huntington's suicide risk is quoted two different ways across the bank - as a 4x (or 4-6x) relative-risk multiplier versus general population, and separately as a 10-15% absolute lifetime risk (up to 12.7%, rising after age 50, and the 3rd commonest cause of death after pneumonia/cardiovascular disease) - read whether the question wants a relative or absolute figure.

source.file: question_bank/Clinical Parts_ Paper B/MCQs Liaison Part 2_ Attempt review.pdf

items.text: The single most common behavioural change in Huntington's disease is lack of initiative, not disinhibition, aggression, or agitation - those are more prevalent-sounding but not the top-ranked finding (Craufurd 2001).

source.file: question_bank/Clinical Parts_ Paper B/MCQs Liaison Part 2_ Attempt review.pdf

blocks.text: **HD** dementia is **SUBCORTICAL** (vs Alzheimer's cortical pattern): early and disproportionate executive dysfunction, with language, visuospatial function, and semantic memory relatively preserved until late - the opposite profile from Alzheimer's disease.

source.file: question_bank/Clinical Parts_ Paper B/MCQs Liaison Part 2_ Attempt review.pdf

blocks.text: Genetic testing for **HD** is advised even in the absence of a known family history, since sporadic new mutations occur.

source.file: question_bank/Clinical Parts_ Paper B/MCQs Liaison Part 2_ Attempt review.pdf

sections.title: 12. Wilson's Disease, Fahr's Disease & Meige Syndrome

blocks.text: Wilson's disease: exclusively psychiatric presentation in 20% of cases; 50% have mental disturbance at some point (personality change, mood abnormality, cognitive dysfunction most common); psychiatric manifestations occur more with neurological than hepatic forms. Cognitive impairment in up to 25% (frontosubcortical pattern); depression in 30%; suicidal behaviour in 4-16%; psychosis is rare (~2%) but can be the initial presentation (Ring & Serra-Mestres 2002).

source.file: books/7-3-liaison-psychiatry.pdf

blocks.text: Kayser-Fleischer rings (corneal copper deposits) are present in 95% of patients with neurological symptoms, 50-60% without neurological symptoms, and only 10% of asymptomatic siblings. **MRI** can show the "giant panda sign" (midbrain hyperintensity sparing the red nucleus/superior colliculus/part of the substantia nigra, with aqueduct hypointensity). Copper-chelating/depleting treatment can improve most manifestations if started early.

source.file: books/7-3-liaison-psychiatry.pdf

blocks.title: Kayser-Fleischer ring prevalence in Wilson's disease by patient group

blocks.text: Fahr's disease: idiopathic basal-ganglia calcium deposition; onset 20-40 years old associates with schizophreniform psychosis/catatonic symptoms, while onset 40-60 associates with dementia and choreoathetosis. 50% have psychiatric problems, correlating with more extensive calcification; depression common, mania much less so; frontosubcortical cognitive pattern. Radiological calcification without clinical features occurs at ~0.9% on **CT**; **MRI** shows striatal hypointensity; **EEG** is non-specific.

source.file: books/7-3-liaison-psychiatry.pdf

blocks.text: Meige syndrome (oral facial dystonia, repetitive blinking and chin thrusting, first described by Henri Meige 1904): more common in women, usually middle age; primary form is idiopathic, secondary form caused by antipsychotics, **levodopa**, or Lewy body dementia. Present both at rest and when active; disappears with sleep.

source.file: books/7-3-liaison-psychiatry.pdf

blocks.text: Meige syndrome is more common in **WOMEN**, not men - the option asking "which statement is incorrect" marks the male-predominance claim as the false one.

source.file: question_bank/Clinical Parts_ Paper B/MCQs Liaison Part 2_ Attempt review.pdf

blocks.text: **TGA** diagnostic criteria: witnessed attack with a capable observer present; clear-cut anterograde amnesia; no clouding of consciousness/loss of identity; cognitive impairment limited to amnesia (no aphasia/apraxia); no focal neurological signs; no epileptic features; resolution within 24 hours; excludes recent head injury or active epilepsy.

source.file: books/7-3-liaison-psychiatry.pdf

expansion: Witnessed attack by a capable observer

blocks.text: Incidence 5-10/100,000/year, rising to 30/100,000 over age 50. Most cases involve hypoperfusion in temporal/parietotemporal regions, particularly the left hemisphere. Patients are mildly confused with intact sensorium and lack insight; episodes last 6-24 hours with high recurrence but usually complete recovery.

source.file: books/7-3-liaison-psychiatry.pdf

blocks.text: **TGA** also produces retrograde amnesia in addition to anterograde amnesia; patients appear calm but bewildered; the episode is most severe in the initial 1-2 hours and by definition must not exceed 24 hours total duration.

source.file: question_bank/Clinical Parts_ Paper B/MCQs Liaison Part 1_ Attempt review.pdf

blocks.text: The most common cause of viral and limbic encephalitis, affecting temporal lobe/limbic circuit; 70% caused by **HSV-1** (immunocompromised patients may have **HSV-2**, **HHV-6**/7). Abrupt confusion, memory impairment, often seizures; 70% show psychiatric disturbance (acute confusion, depression, psychosis); fever common but not invariable.

source.file: books/7-3-liaison-psychiatry.pdf

blocks.text: Imaging shows signal change/swelling in the temporal lobes (visible on **CT**, better seen on **MRI**, the imaging of choice); **CSF** shows lymphocytosis and raised protein; gold-standard diagnosis is **CSF** **PCR** for herpes viruses (~95% sensitivity/specificity). **EEG** is invariably abnormal - non-specific slowing early, high-voltage periodic lateralizing epileptiform discharges later (diagnostically useful if present, but not **HSE**-specific).

source.file: books/7-3-liaison-psychiatry.pdf

blocks.text: **CT**/**MRI** in **HSE** shows signal change and swelling in the **TEMPORAL** lobes specifically - a deliberate "except" distractor substitutes frontal lobes as the wrong location.

source.file: question_bank/Clinical Parts_ Paper B/MCQs Liaison Part 1_ Attempt review.pdf

blocks.text: Untreated case fatality is ~70%; **IV** aciclovir reduces this to 20-30%; treatment should continue for at least 14 days, longer if immunocompromised.

source.file: books/7-3-liaison-psychiatry.pdf

blocks.text: **HSE** is the most common human cause of Kluver-Bucy syndrome (emotional blunting, hyperphagia, visual agnosia, inappropriate sexual behaviour) from bilateral temporal lobe damage (usually only a partial syndrome); **carbamazepine** may control some symptoms.

source.file: books/7-3-liaison-psychiatry.pdf

blocks.text: **HSE** most commonly causes amnesia (vs bacterial/**TB** meningitis, cerebral lupus, **HIV** encephalitis); personality change and focal seizures also feature; the virus enters via the nasopharynx and preferentially attacks the temporal lobes; **HSV** is the most common cause of sporadic (non-epidemic) viral encephalitis. **HSV-1** predominates in adults/children over 3 months; **HSV-2** in neonates (acquired at delivery).

source.file: question_bank/Clinical Parts_ Paper B/MCQs Liaison Part 1_ Attempt review.pdf

blocks.text: The clinical feature most suggestive of **HSE** is abrupt-onset confusion (as opposed to chorea, anxiety, myoclonus, or dystonia, which point elsewhere).

source.file: question_bank/Clinical Parts_ Paper B/MCQs Liaison Part 2_ Attempt review.pdf

blocks.text: Peak incidence of head injury is age 15-24. Concussion causes transient coma followed by apparent recovery; contusion causes prolonged coma, focal signs, lasting damage - though pathological support for this division is poor. **TBI** mechanisms: shearing/rotational stress (contrecoup), direct trauma, oedema/raised **ICP**, hypoxia/ischaemia.

source.file: books/7-3-liaison-psychiatry.pdf

blocks.text: Post-traumatic amnesia (**PTA**, anterograde, from injury until normal memory resumes) durations map to severity/outcome: <60min = mild (return to work <1 month); 1-24h = moderate (<2 months); 1-7 days = severe (<4 months); >7 days = very severe (>1 year). Retrograde amnesia (dense amnesia before injury) generally reduces over minutes.

source.file: books/7-3-liaison-psychiatry.pdf

blocks.title: Post-traumatic amnesia (PTA) duration, injury severity, and functional outcome
rows: May return to work in <1 month
May return to work in 2 months
May return to work in 4 months
May require >1 year for return to work

blocks.text: Poor psychiatric-morbidity prognostic factors: long **LOC**/**PTA**, elderly, chronic alcohol use, diffuse brain damage, new-onset seizures, focal damage to the **DOMINANT** lobe. **LOC**/**PTA** are more predictive of functional outcome than **GCS**; **AIS** predicts survival.

source.file: books/7-3-liaison-psychiatry.pdf

blocks.text: Depression is the most common late sequela (with anxiety, roughly 1/4 of survivors); left-frontal lesion proximity predicts depression. Schizophrenia-like psychosis with prominent paranoia links to left temporal injury; affective psychosis (mania in 9%) links to right temporal/orbitofrontal injury. Schizophrenia incidence increases post-head-injury (~2.5% develop it). Post-traumatic epilepsy occurs in 5% of closed and 30% of open injuries, usually in year one, worsening prognosis. Children show less psychopathology due to greater brain plasticity.

source.file: books/7-3-liaison-psychiatry.pdf

blocks.text: Post-concussion syndrome follows mild (**PTA**<1h, **GCS** 13-15, **LOC**<15min) or moderate (**PTA** 1-24h, **GCS** 9-12, **LOC** 15min-6h) head injury; symptoms include headache, dizziness, fatigue, poor memory/concentration, irritability, depression, sleep disturbance, photophobia, tinnitus. At least 50% recover fully within 3 months; slower recovery with age >40, prior head injury, or alcohol/substance misuse. Early intervention (a single hour-long assessment/treatment session with education plus reassurance) significantly reduces persisting symptoms.

source.file: books/7-3-liaison-psychiatry.pdf

blocks.text: Poor prognostic factors are long **PTA**, long **LOC**, older age, and chronic alcohol use - focal damage to the **NON**-dominant lobe is specifically **NOT** a poor-prognosis factor (dominant-lobe damage is), a common except-question trap.

source.file: question_bank/Clinical Parts_ Paper B/MCQs Liaison Part 2_ Attempt review.pdf

blocks.text: Poor prognosis after head injury is linked to focal damage of the **DOMINANT** lobe - damage to the non-dominant lobe is deliberately offered as the incorrect "except" answer.

source.file: question_bank/Clinical Parts_ Paper B/MCQs Liaison Part 2_ Attempt review.pdf

blocks.text: The cognitive faculty most affected in post-concussion syndrome is speed of information processing (attention deficits, difficulty with complex tasks) - not visual memory, line orientation, digit span, or time perception.

source.file: question_bank/Clinical Parts_ Paper B/MCQs Liaison Part 1_ Attempt review.pdf

blocks.text: Head injury (especially in men) may predispose to Alzheimer's disease via beta-amyloid deposition at the injury site (**APOE** link inconsistent); head injury as a schizophrenia risk factor remains contested (David & Prince 2005) even though psychosis is a recognised post-injury complication.

source.file: question_bank/Clinical Parts_ Paper B/MCQs Liaison Part 2_ Attempt review.pdf

blocks.text: **ICSD** divides dyssomnias (primary insomnia/hypersomnia, circadian sleep disorders, narcolepsy, breathing-related disorders, sleep-state misperception) from parasomnias, subdivided by sleep phase: **NREM** arousal disorders (confusional arousals, sleepwalking, sleep terrors), sleep-wake transition disorders (sleep starts, sleep talking), and **REM** parasomnias (**REM** behavioural disorder, nightmares, sleep paralysis). Other parasomnias include bruxism and enuresis.

source.file: books/7-3-liaison-psychiatry.pdf

blocks.text: Delayed sleep phase syndrome (most common circadian disorder): inability to fall asleep until very early morning, progressively delaying over time. Narcolepsy: prevalence 0.025%; excessive daytime sleepiness/sleep attacks, cataplexy (75%), sleep paralysis (30%), hypnagogic hallucinations (only 10% have all four features); associated with **HLA-DQB1*0602** and low **CSF** hypocretin-1 (orexin-A); sleep polysomnogram shows sleep latency <10 min with sleep-onset **REM**. Stimulants (**methylphenidate**, **modafinil**) treat sleepiness; **imipramine** may help cataplexy.

source.file: books/7-3-liaison-psychiatry.pdf

blocks.text: Obstructive sleep apnoea more common in men (4%) than women (2.5%); snoring is the most common presenting symptom; untreated cases risk right-sided cardiac failure. Sleepwalking arises from slow-wave (stage 3/4) sleep, mostly in the first third of the night; sleep terrors similarly occur in stages 3/4 **NREM** in the first third of the night, with panicky screaming, no recall, and unresponsiveness during the episode.

source.file: books/7-3-liaison-psychiatry.pdf

blocks.text: **REM** sleep behaviour disorder: loss of normal **REM** atonia, dreams acted out (sometimes violently); occurs in the middle-to-latter third of the night; may be idiopathic or prodromal to Parkinson's disease, Lewy body dementia, multiple system atrophy, Guillain-Barre syndrome (associated lesions likely in the brainstem). **Clonazepam** is effective treatment; making the sleep environment safe is first-line.

source.file: books/7-3-liaison-psychiatry.pdf

blocks.text: Restless legs syndrome (age ≥12): akathisia-like urge to move legs (core feature) with paraesthesias, motor restlessness, symptoms worse at rest and at night; an awake phenomenon; prevalence 3-15% (median 7.2%), M:F 1:2, familial pattern in >50% of primary cases. Predisposing factors include iron deficiency (check ferritin/iron saturation), peripheral neuropathy, sedating antihistamines, dopamine antagonists (metoclopramide, prochlorperazine), antipsychotics, caffeine, most antidepressants (except **bupropion**). Treatment: sleep hygiene, non-ergot dopamine agonists (**ropinirole** - first licensed - **pramipexole**), anticonvulsants (**gabapentin**, **carbamazepine**), opioids, **clonazepam**; oral iron if ferritin low.

source.file: books/7-3-liaison-psychiatry.pdf

blocks.text: Periodic limb movement disorder is an **ASLEEP** phenomenon (contrast with **RLS**, an awake phenomenon), diagnosed by polysomnography; **PLMS** occur in up to 34% of people over 60, and are common in **RLS** (80-90%), narcolepsy (45-65%), and **REM** behaviour disorder (70%); dopaminergic impairment and iron deficiency implicated, as in **RLS**. Pharmacological treatment is not warranted unless there is clear sleep disruption.

source.file: books/7-3-liaison-psychiatry.pdf

blocks.text: Periodic limb movement disorder is an **ASLEEP** phenomenon, unlike restless legs syndrome which is an **AWAKE** phenomenon - the two conditions are repeatedly contrasted and their awake/asleep labels swapped as distractors.

source.file: question_bank/Clinical Parts_ Paper B/MCQs Liaison Part 2_ Attempt review.pdf

blocks.text: Initial insomnia (increased sleep latency) is linked to anxiety disorders; middle insomnia (fragmented sleep) is linked to medical illness/pain/depression; terminal insomnia (early morning wakening) is linked to major depression.

source.file: books/7-3-liaison-psychiatry.pdf

blocks.text: Nightmares are more common in females; **REM** sleep behaviour disorder is more common in males over 50; no gender difference is reported for sleepwalking, sleep terrors, or confusional arousals.

source.file: question_bank/Clinical Parts_ Paper B/MCQs Liaison Part 1_ Attempt review.pdf

blocks.text: Sleep terrors occur in **NREM** slow-wave (stage 3/4) sleep in the first third of the night, with autonomic hyperactivity that includes tachycardia, tachypnoea, diaphoresis, flushed face, dilated pupils, **AND** increased muscle tone (not the acting-out/vivid-recall pattern of **REM** behaviour disorder), lasting 5-10 minutes with no dream recall.

source.file: question_bank/Clinical Parts_ Paper B/MCQs Liaison Part 1_ Attempt review.pdf

blocks.text: Sleep terrors specifically feature **INCREASED** muscle tone alongside autonomic hyperactivity - this is the marked-correct answer, not the acting-out/vivid-dream-recall pattern that belongs to **REM** sleep behaviour disorder.

source.file: question_bank/Clinical Parts_ Paper B/MCQs Liaison Part 1_ Attempt review.pdf

blocks.text: **CFS** prevalence: **US** community samples 0.23-0.42%, **UK** sample 2.6% falling to 0.5% after excluding comorbid psychological disease. Higher in women (M:F 1:3), lower occupational/educational status; mean onset age 29-35; mean duration 3-9 years; lower prevalence but still diagnosed in children/adolescents.

source.file: books/7-3-liaison-psychiatry.pdf

blocks.text: **US** **CDC** (1994) criteria: persistent/relapsing unexplained chronic fatigue of new onset lasting ≥6 months, not explained by organic disease or continuing exertion, not relieved by rest, plus ≥4 of: impaired memory/concentration, sore throat, tender lymph nodes, muscle pain, multi-joint pain, new headaches, unrefreshing sleep, post-exertional malaise. Excludes major psychiatric disorders (psychotic depression, bipolar, schizophrenia, dementia, eating disorders, substance misuse) - but non-psychotic psychiatric disorders are **NOT** exclusion criteria.

source.file: books/7-3-liaison-psychiatry.pdf

blocks.text: Predictors of poor outcome (Powell 2004): claiming disability benefit, low sense of control, strong focus on physical symptoms, passivity with reduced activity, self-help group membership (an indicator of perceived severity, not a cause). Severity and duration of illness are **NOT** useful predictors of treatment response.

source.file: books/7-3-liaison-psychiatry.pdf

blocks.text: 33% of **CFS** patients are unable to work, 33% work only part-time. **NICE** red-flag symptoms suggesting an alternative serious illness: significant weight loss, significant lymphadenopathy, focal neurological signs, inflammatory arthritis/connective tissue/cardiorespiratory disease features, sleep apnoea.

source.file: books/7-3-liaison-psychiatry.pdf

blocks.text: Aetiology is multifactorial: predisposing (neuroticism, childhood inactivity/illness), precipitating (infectious mononucleosis, Q fever, Lyme disease, life events), perpetuating (belief in physical cause, activity avoidance, poor self-control, primary/secondary gain, low self-perceived cognitive ability). **HPA**-axis and serotonin-pathway abnormality is the most consistent finding; 1/3 have hypocortisolism of **CNS** (not primary adrenal) origin; family studies suggest cortisol-transporting-globulin mutation.

source.file: books/7-3-liaison-psychiatry.pdf

blocks.text: **CBT** and graded exercise therapy are the only evidence-based treatments; **CBT** is not a cure but its effect can last up to 5 years in responders (Deale 2001) by targeting cognitive/behavioural drivers (misperceived cause, activity avoidance, excessive rest). Medication added to **CBT** improved outcomes, but **CBT** added to medication did not - timing matters (Stubhaug 2008).

source.file: books/7-3-liaison-psychiatry.pdf

blocks.text: **CBT** vs graded exercise therapy (**GET**): **CBT** is behavioural/avoidance-model-based, always includes graded activity, ~70% improvement, more complex training; **GET** is deconditioning-model-based, doesn't specifically treat cognition (though some studies add cognitive work), ~55% improvement, less complex training. Antidepressants should not be used routinely in **CFS**; if used, severity-guided, mindful that prolonged inactivity raises autonomic side-effect risk and sedation can worsen fatigue.

source.file: books/7-3-liaison-psychiatry.pdf

blocks.title: CBT versus graded exercise therapy (GET) for CFS
rows: Not specifically treated (some studies add cognitive work)

blocks.text: Pacing balances rest and activity to avoid a "boom and bust" cycle; recommended by patient groups but effectiveness is questionable and **NICE** includes it only on consensus grounds; it might prolong illness by encouraging avoidance.

source.file: books/7-3-liaison-psychiatry.pdf

blocks.text: Prognosis: full spontaneous recovery is rare; 17-65% improve over 5 years, <10% recover over 5 years, 10-20% worsen. **CFS** is not associated with increased mortality. 23% have current major depression, 50-75% lifetime history (Wessley 1998); **CFS**/depression differ on serotonergic direction (**CNS** upregulation vs downregulation), symptom pattern, **HPA** axis direction, sleep pattern, and antidepressant response (not effective in pure **CFS** vs effective in depression).

source.file: books/7-3-liaison-psychiatry.pdf

blocks.title: CFS versus depression: distinguishing features
rows: Absence of guilt/anhedonia; sore throat, adenopathy, post-exertional fatigue present
Absence of sore throat/adenopathy/post-exertional fatigue; guilt and anhedonia present

blocks.text: Panic disorder lifetime prevalence in **CFS** 17-25%; **GAD** lifetime prevalence 2-30%; **CFS** is **NOT** simply a physical presentation of anxiety despite overlapping cerebral-blood-flow/sympathetic/sleep abnormalities. Somatisation rate in **CFS** is 28% and is attribution-dependent (higher if the examiner attributes symptoms psychologically). 20-70% of fibromyalgia patients meet **CFS** criteria and vice versa (35-70%); overlaps also exist with multiple chemical sensitivity, **IBS**, **TMJ** disorder.

source.file: books/7-3-liaison-psychiatry.pdf

blocks.text: The diagnostic duration criterion for **CFS** is 6 months, not >12 months - a deliberate except-question trap.

source.file: question_bank/Clinical Parts_ Paper B/MCQs Liaison Part 1_ Attempt review.pdf

blocks.text: The **CFS** diagnostic duration criterion is 6 months, not the intuitively "safer-sounding" >12 months - a classic except-question distractor.

source.file: question_bank/Clinical Parts_ Paper B/MCQs Liaison Part 1_ Attempt review.pdf

blocks.text: Significant weight loss is specifically **NOT** characteristic of **CFS** (the marked-incorrect option in an except-question); unemployment rates in **CFS** are 35-69%.

source.file: question_bank/Clinical Parts_ Paper B/MCQs Liaison Part 1_ Attempt review.pdf

blocks.text: Significant weight loss is specifically **NOT** characteristic of **CFS** - it is a **NICE** red-flag symptom that should instead prompt investigation for an alternative serious illness, making it the correct "except" answer.

source.file: question_bank/Clinical Parts_ Paper B/MCQs Liaison Part 1_ Attempt review.pdf

blocks.note: The book notes cite older **CDC** (1994) diagnostic criteria and older graded-exercise-therapy evidence. **NICE** **NG206** (2021) substantially revised **UK** guidance on **CFS**/**ME**, notably de-emphasising **GET** as a curative treatment - this guide reflects only the **SPMM** source material's (older) framing. Cross-check current **NICE** guidance before relying on the **GET**/**CBT** efficacy figures here for exam answers that specify "current **NICE** guidance".

blocks.text: **DSM-5** replaced pain disorder/somatization disorder/hypochondriasis/undifferentiated somatoform disorder with Somatic Symptom and Related Disorders (**SSD**) - diagnosed on **POSITIVE** symptoms/signs (distressing somatic symptoms plus abnormal thoughts/feelings/behaviours), not on absence of a medical explanation.

source.file: books/7-3-liaison-psychiatry.pdf

blocks.text: Pain is the most common presenting somatic symptom in medical outpatients; depression occurs in 10-15% of pain-disorder patients (also common: substance misuse, **PTSD**, Geisser 1996); 43% of depressed adults report pain (Ohayon & Schatzberg 2003). Treatments improving depression give moderate reductions in pain severity/disability via a shared central pain-modulation mechanism. **CBT** for chronic pain works best with cognitive restructuring, relaxation training, time-based activity pacing, and graded homework against avoidance.

source.file: books/7-3-liaison-psychiatry.pdf

blocks.text: Atypical/persistent idiopathic facial pain (Frazier & Russell 1924; **IHS** 2004 criteria): unilateral, poorly localised, present most of the day, described as severe ache/crushing/burning, not fitting any cranial neuralgia, no sensory loss or imaging/lab abnormality. Depression and anxiety are prevalent; treatment requires a difficult multidisciplinary approach.

source.file: books/7-3-liaison-psychiatry.pdf

blocks.text: **BAP** guidelines (Cleare 2015): there is a lack of compelling evidence that SNRIs are more effective than SSRIs for pain symptoms associated with depression, and no clinically useful predictive biological factor for antidepressant response has been identified.

source.file: books/7-3-liaison-psychiatry.pdf

blocks.text: **HIV**-associated acute stress reaction typically occurs on informing someone of seropositivity or transition to full **AIDS** - brooding about the future, panic attacks, social isolation, rage, or desperation appearing within minutes-to-hours and remitting within 2-3 days.

source.file: books/7-3-liaison-psychiatry.pdf

blocks.text: Adjustment disorder with anxiety/depressed mood occurs in 5-20% of **HIV**-infected patients. Anxiety symptoms/disorders occur in 11-25%; "worried well" describes seronegative high-risk individuals whose anxiety about infection can progress to **GAD**, panic disorder, **OCD**, or hypochondriasis despite repeated negative tests.

source.file: books/7-3-liaison-psychiatry.pdf

blocks.text: Depression is the most common **HIV** psychiatric disorder - ~40% (30-60% lifetime), higher in women, and became the most common cause of psychiatric hospitalisation in some countries post-**HAART**. High-risk groups for **HIV** (**STD** history, homosexual men, lower socioeconomic groups) also independently carry higher depression risk; some depression criteria (poor sleep, weight loss) overlap with **HIV** symptoms, spuriously inflating rates. Suicide risk factors include **AIDS**-related bereavement, recent seropositivity notification, relapse, social difficulties around homosexuality, poor support, and comorbid dementia/delirium.

source.file: books/7-3-liaison-psychiatry.pdf

blocks.text: TCAs and SSRIs are equally effective for **HIV** depression; SSRIs are safer in overdose with fewer side effects and can be started at 25% of the usual dose. Secondary-amine TCAs (desipramine, **nortriptyline**) are preferred, reserved for asymptomatic illness; **AIDS** patients respond to lower **TCA** doses (25-100mg) but may still get severe anticholinergic effects. Interpersonal psychotherapy is particularly beneficial; combining psychotherapy with medication may be optimal (Markowitz).

source.file: books/7-3-liaison-psychiatry.pdf

blocks.text: Psychotic symptoms are usually late-stage, uncommon, and may reflect direct neurotoxicity, iatrogenic causes, or substance misuse. **AIDS** patients on typical antipsychotics are particularly prone to extrapyramidal side effects and **NMS**; **risperidone** may be tolerated even after standard neuroleptics had to be stopped for **EPSE**.

source.file: books/7-3-liaison-psychiatry.pdf

blocks.text: Mania is the most frequent reason for psychiatric hospitalisation in **HIV** (ahead of depression, then psychosis); associated with illicit drug use and iatrogenic causes (especially didanosine, ganciclovir, procarbazine, stavudine, steroids, zidovudine), mostly in advanced disease with cognitive impairment. New-onset mania in advanced symptomatic disease predicts reduced survival. **Lithium**/**valproate** can cause neurological toxicity; **carbamazepine** requires strict haemopoietic monitoring given concurrent **AZT** risk.

source.file: books/7-3-liaison-psychiatry.pdf

blocks.text: Delirium is one of the most frequent organic mental disorders in hospitalised **HIV** patients and is probably underdiagnosed; acute causes on top of **HIV** must always be excluded.

source.file: books/7-3-liaison-psychiatry.pdf

blocks.text: **AIDS** dementia complex: **WHO** (1990) distinguished **HIV**-associated dementia from mild cognitive/motor disorder (largely intact ADLs). Present at initial **AIDS** diagnosis in 3% of cases; incidence 7%/year in the first 2 years post-**AIDS** diagnosis; 15% develop dementia over the disease course. Risk factors: older age, decreased body mass, low haematocrit, **IV** drug use history.

source.file: books/7-3-liaison-psychiatry.pdf

blocks.text: Early **HIV** dementia: cognitive slowing/forgetfulness, apathy/social withdrawal, depression/irritability/lability. Later stages: global cognitive deterioration, severe psychomotor retardation, mutism, paraparesis, bladder/bowel incontinence, myoclonus, seizures. Naming/vocabulary are preserved even late, consistent with a subcortical dementia pattern; bilateral ring-enhancing lesions on imaging suggest cerebral toxoplasmosis, while contrast-enhancing mass lesions suggest primary **CNS** lymphoma.

blocks.mnemonic: "CAME" on early - Cognitive, Apathy, Motor, Emotional
expansion: Cognitive: forgetfulness, mental slowing, reduced sequential-task performance
Apathy: reduced spontaneity/emotional responsivity, social withdrawal
Motor: loss of balance/coordination, clumsiness, leg weakness
Emotional: depression, irritability/lability, agitation, occasional psychosis

blocks.text: **CSF** markers predictive of **HIV** dementia: raised beta-2-microglobulin and neopterin, and **CD4** count; **HIV** **RNA** in **CSF** correlates with dementia severity. Zidovudine (reverse-transcriptase inhibitor) has some evidence for preventing cognitive decline; didanosine appears not to affect progression; no trial data on protease inhibitors (poor **CSF** penetration). **Methylphenidate** (10-90mg/day) has repeatedly improved cognitive symptoms with relatively mild side effects.

source.file: books/7-3-liaison-psychiatry.pdf

blocks.text: Secondary organic brain diseases in **HIV**: progressive multifocal leucoencephalopathy (rapid dementia, no treatment, rapid death); cerebral toxoplasmosis (basal-ganglia lesions, multiple ring-like calcified lesions on imaging, treated with pyrimethamine/sulphadiazine); cryptococcal meningitis (headache, meningism, fever, delirium, treated with **IV** amphotericin B); primary **CNS** lymphoma (up to 10% of **AIDS** patients, almost always **EBV**-associated, presenting with seizures/personality change/focal deficits without fever).

source.file: books/7-3-liaison-psychiatry.pdf

blocks.text: Antiretroviral psychiatric effects: zidovudine can cause confusion, agitation, insomnia, mania, depression; stavudine/didanosine/zalcitabine cause peripheral neuropathy, and mania is specifically associated with didanosine; efavirenz causes significant neuropsychiatric effects (46% develop them - a third depression, 2% psychosis - and ~6% stop the drug because of them).

source.file: books/7-3-liaison-psychiatry.pdf

blocks.text: Interpersonal psychotherapy (not **DBT**, mentalisation, standard **CBT**, or psychodynamic therapy) has the established evidence base for **HIV**-associated depression (Markowitz 1998).

blocks.text: Hypochondriasis's most common comorbidity is **GAD** (71%), then dysthymia (45.2%), **MDD** (42.9%), somatisation disorder (21.4%), panic disorder (16.7%); 88% have at least one comorbid psychiatric disorder and patients are 3x more likely to have a personality disorder than the general population.

blocks.text: Suicide risk within 1 year of deliberate self-harm (**DSH**) is ~0.7% overall (1.1% males, 0.5% females) - about 66x general-population risk; roughly 1% die by completed suicide within 24 months of the index parasuicidal act, with risk highest in the weeks immediately following, representing 50-100x general-population mortality.

blocks.text: Completed-suicide risk factors: male sex (female sex is the marked-incorrect/"except" option), older age, single/divorced/widowed, living alone with poor social support, unemployment/low socioeconomic status, previous **DSH**, any mental disorder (greatest risk with major depression and anorexia nervosa, then functional psychosis, then neurotic/personality disorders), alcohol/drug dependence, recent psychiatric admission, and concurrent physical illness.

blocks.text: Late-pregnancy **SSRI** exposure most often causes neonatal irritability/discontinuation symptoms (not neural tube defects, facial abnormalities, Ebstein's anomaly, or neonatal bleeding as the primary risk); short-half-life drugs (**paroxetine**, **venlafaxine**) carry higher discontinuation-symptom risk. Persistent pulmonary hypertension of the newborn risk is increased but the absolute risk remains very low; postpartum haemorrhage risk is also increased.

blocks.text: **MADRS** is used for observer-rated antidepressant response monitoring (response ≥50% reduction from baseline, remission ≤10); the Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale (**EPDS**) is for postpartum screening specifically, not for tracking treatment response.

blocks.text: For bipolar relapse prevention while breastfeeding, sodium **valproate** is preferred over **lithium**/**lorazepam**/**lofepramine**/chloral hydrate; **lithium** in breast milk risks infant thyroid dysfunction, cyanosis, poor tone, and **ECG** change, with reduced infant renal clearance for up to 5 months. A single case report links **valproate** via breast milk to serious blood dyscrasia, so LFTs/platelets should be monitored.

source.file: question_bank/Clinical Parts_ Paper B/MCQs Liaison Part 1_ Attempt review.pdf

blocks.text: First-trimester bipolar relapse prevention: **NICE** recommends switching to an antipsychotic (e.g. **olanzapine**) rather than **lithium**, **valproate**, **valproate**+**lithium**, or **lamotrigine**, since no mood stabiliser is clearly safe in the first trimester.

source.file: question_bank/Clinical Parts_ Paper B/MCQs Liaison Part 1_ Attempt review.pdf

blocks.text: Folate does not prevent anticonvulsant-induced neural tube defects if only started once pregnancy has begun (it may help if given pre-conception), but folate should always be offered for its separate neurodevelopmental benefit.

source.file: question_bank/Clinical Parts_ Paper B/MCQs Liaison Part 1_ Attempt review.pdf

blocks.text: **Fluoxetine** is preferred over **paroxetine**, **sertraline**, **citalopram**, and **venlafaxine** for depression in pregnancy per the Maudsley Guidelines (most evidence, safer than **paroxetine**).

blocks.text: Relapse of psychotic illness (schizophrenia) postpartum occurs in ~16% within 12 months in women with known schizophrenia - a less common and different pattern from postpartum relapse risk in bipolar disorder.

blocks.text: "Baby blues" affects up to 3/4 of new mothers, onset day 2-3 postpartum, lasting 1-2 days, weakly linked to the postpartum drop in oestrogen/progesterone/prolactin around 72 hours after birth.

blocks.text: The maximum **valproate** dose in pregnancy if continuation is essential is 1000mg/day (**NICE**); anticonvulsant-as-mood-stabiliser withdrawal should be tapered over a minimum of 1 month (vs 6 months when the same drug is used for epilepsy).

blocks.text: **Modafinil** acts by blocking the dopamine transporter, increasing synaptic dopamine, which activates orexin/hypocretin-releasing hypothalamic neurons and downstream histamine release from the tuberomammillary nucleus; its elimination half-life is 10-12 hours (not 24h); headache is the most common (dose-dependent) side effect; it can theoretically activate psychosis, mania, or suicidal ideation.
